points: A data model is a human-readable way of modeling database tables, where tables are called objects, columns are called fields, and rows are called records.
Salesforce supports several object types: standard, custom, external, platform events, and Big Objects; the module focuses on standard and custom.
Standard objects are included with Salesforce, such as Account, Contact, Lead, and Opportunity.
Custom objects store information specific to a company or industry; for DreamHouse, the custom Property object stores homes for sale.
Creating a custom object automatically builds its user interface page layout.
Every standard and custom object has identity, system, and name fields, plus any custom fields you add.
Identity fields are 18-character case-insensitive IDs, with a 15-character case-sensitive version, and appear in a record's URL.
System fields are read-only and record information like CreatedDate, LastModifiedById, and LastModifiedDate.
Name fields can be text or auto-numbered, such as CA-1024 for a support case.
Custom fields are created on standard or custom objects, and their API names end in __c.
Every field has a data type that defines what kind of information it stores.
Checkbox fields store yes/no values, Date and DateTime fields store dates and times, and Formula fields calculate values from a written formula.
Good object and field naming is descriptive and unique, avoiding lazy names like Property2.
Adding descriptions and help text improves clarity for users.
Required fields prevent incomplete data on important records.
principles: Model business data as objects, fields, and records so it matches how people think about the information.
Use standard objects for common business entities and custom objects for company-specific data.
Choose each field's data type based on the kind of information it needs to store.
Name objects and fields descriptively and uniquely so the org stays clear as it grows.
Document customizations with descriptions and help text, and require fields that must always be filled.

points: Apex is a hosted, server-side, Java-like language on the Salesforce Platform that works like database stored procedures.
Apex is object-oriented, strongly typed, multitenant-aware, case-insensitive, versioned, and easy to unit test.
Apex-only features include triggers, the global access modifier, transactions with rollback, and versioned custom code.
Apex data types: primitives (Integer, Double, Long, Date, Datetime, String, ID, Boolean), sObjects, collections (List, Set, Map), enums, user-defined classes, and system classes.
Lists are ordered, indexed, and allow duplicates. Use add() to append. Square brackets read by index but cannot add elements.
Static methods are called on the class name without an instance. They cannot use instance member variables.
Anonymous Apex runs code on the fly in the Developer Console (Debug > Execute Anonymous) and generates debug logs.
System.debug() writes values to the debug log, which can be filtered with Debug Only in the Log Inspector.
An sObject is the in-memory representation of a Salesforce record. Creating one with new does not save it to the database.
Fields can be populated with constructor name-value pairs (fastest) or dot notation. Account requires Name before insert.
API names: custom objects and fields end in __c, custom relationship fields end in __r, and spaces become underscores.
A generic sObject variable can hold any record type, but its fields are accessed only with get() and put(). Cast it to a specific type to use dot notation.
DML statements (insert, update, upsert, delete, undelete, merge) create and modify records. DML cannot retrieve records; SOQL does that.
Upsert matches on record ID by default, or on an idLookup field (standard) or external ID field (custom). Zero matches inserts, one match updates, and multiple matches throw an error.
Bulk DML on lists is recommended. Each DML statement counts toward the 150-per-transaction governor limit, regardless of list size.

Database class methods mirror DML. allOrNone=false allows partial success and returns SaveResult, UpsertResult, or DeleteResult objects. The default allOrNone=true behaves like DML and throws on failure.
Related records: set the foreign key (such as AccountId) on insert. Updates to parent and child need separate DML calls. Deleting a parent cascades to its children.
SOQL syntax is SELECT fields FROM Object [WHERE] [ORDER BY] [LIMIT]. Inline SOQL is written in square brackets. Apex always returns Id. SELECT * is not supported.
SOQL string comparisons are case-insensitive. LIKE uses % for any or no characters and _ for exactly one character. Bind variables use a colon prefix.
Child records are queried with an inner SELECT on the relationship name. Parent fields are traversed with dot notation, such as Account.Name.
SOQL for loops process up to 200 sObjects per batch, which avoids heap limits on large result sets.
SOSL performs word-based text search across many objects at once, similar to Apache Lucene. SOQL queries a single object with exact matching.
SOSL syntax: FIND 'term' [IN SearchGroup] [RETURNING ObjectsAndFields] in Apex, and FIND {term} in Query Editor. The default search group is ALL FIELDS.
SOSL wildcards: * matches zero or more characters and ? matches exactly one character, in the middle or end of a term. AND, OR, and phrases in double quotes are supported.
principles: Apex is a server-side, data-focused language. Business logic runs in the cloud, close to the data.
Creating an sObject in memory and persisting it to the database are separate steps. DML persists and SOQL retrieves.
Always use bulk operations on lists and stay within governor limits such as the 150 DML statements per transaction.
Use DML statements when any failure should throw an exception. Use Database methods with allOrNone=false when partial success is acceptable and you want to inspect errors.
A transaction is all-or-nothing. If any DML operation fails, all operations in that transaction roll back.
Use upsert with an external ID or idLookup field to avoid duplicates without checking existence first.
Use SOQL for structured queries on one object. Use SOSL for text searches across multiple objects.
Test queries in Query Builder, the Query Editor, or Anonymous Apex before adding them to Apex code.

points: Source: a 2013 Tata Consultancy Services deck on MDM and PLM for enterprise product data (based on a summary of the 16 slides)
Globalization, mergers, and acquisitions spread product data across disconnected systems, causing ownership and governance problems
Duplicate or outdated product data and slow reconciliation make it hard for decision-makers to trust their data
Product MDM traditionally serves sales and marketing needs such as catalogs and pricing
The deck argues product MDM scope should expand to include engineering and manufacturing data
PLM is the authoring space for work-in-progress engineering data
MDM holds released product data as the system of record and feeds it to consumers such as sales, supply chain, and analytics
PLM and MDM are presented as complementary rather than redundant
Key use cases include standards-based metamodel definition, data ownership and access control, and automated data migration from engineering systems
Other use cases include closed-loop engineering change processes and validated integration between engineering and product master systems
Expected benefits include uniform product data, better change management, improved compliance traceability, fewer interfaces, and greater scalability
Lessons learned include slow interface harmonization due to business-unit variations and no standard ownership mechanism
Legacy data conflict resolution and historical migration can be slow and complex, and upstream and downstream changes need heavy coordination
Standards such as STEP, JT2Go, and PLCS should be evaluated
principles: Product data fragmentation caused by globalization and M&A undermines data trust and governance
MDM is the system of record for released product data, while PLM manages work-in-progress engineering data
Product master data management should extend from sales and marketing into engineering and manufacturing
Organizations must define their own data ownership rules because no standard mechanism exists

points: Big objects are defined in Setup by entering 'Big Objects' in Quick Find and selecting Big Objects; defining them with Metadata API is possible but more complex.
Once saved, a big object's API name uses the suffix __b, while a custom object uses __c.
Object names must be unique across standard, custom, external, and big objects in the org.
A new big object starts with the status In Development and can't be deployed until it has an index containing at least one custom field.
Big objects support these field types: Lookup Relationship, Date/Time, Email, Number, Phone, Text, Text Area (Long), and URL.
The index defines the composite primary key of a big object and determines both its identity and which queries are possible.
An index can contain 1 to 5 custom fields, all of which must be marked required.
Long Text Area fields cannot be part of an index, and the total characters across all text fields in an index cannot exceed 100.
Once created, an index cannot be edited or deleted; changing it requires creating a new big object.
With SOQL, you can query only on index fields, in the order they were defined, so the most frequently filtered field goes in Index Position 1.
Index fields can sort Ascending or Descending.
Big objects can be populated with a CSV file through Data Loader, the Bulk API, or the SOAP API, or entirely through Apex using insertImmediate.
Deleted big objects are kept for 15 days, during which they can be restored or permanently deleted.
principles: Plan the index before building the object, because the index cannot be changed later and determines which queries work.
Put the field you filter on most often in the first index position, since SOQL queries must follow index order.
Reinserting a record with an existing index value overwrites that record, which makes inserts idempotent and avoids duplicates, similar to an upsert.
Apex tests that mix DML on big objects with other objects fail, so use the Apex stub API to isolate test DML.

points: Big objects store and manage massive amounts of data on the Salesforce platform, from hundreds of thousands to a billion records or more, with consistent performance.
There are two kinds of big objects: standard big objects, defined by Salesforce within its products, and custom big objects, defined and deployed in Setup.
FieldHistoryArchive is a standard big object, part of Field Audit Trail, that stores up to 10 years of archived field history.
Common custom big object use cases are a 360° view of the customer, auditing and tracking long-term usage, and maintaining a historical archive.
Big objects can be queried with standard SOQL, the Bulk API (for results over 100k records), and batch Apex (for manipulating data).
Batch Apex jobs should self-paginate when operating on result sets larger than 50k records.
Big objects support only object and field permissions.
SOQL relationship queries work only through a lookup field from the big object to a standard or custom object, and only in the select field list, not in filters or subqueries.
Big objects use custom Lightning and Visualforce components instead of standard UI elements such as home pages, detail pages, and list views.
An org can have up to 100 big objects, and field limits are similar to those for custom objects and depend on the license type.
Big objects cannot be used in transactions that also include standard or custom objects.
Triggers, flows, processes, and the Salesforce app are not supported for big objects.
principles: Big objects trade flexibility for scale, so they behave differently from standard and custom objects and require design planning up front.
Choose big objects for very large datasets used for analytics, compliance, or archiving, rather than for everyday transactional records that need full platform features.
Query design matters: the Bulk API suits reporting over very large result sets, while batch Apex suits data manipulation.

points: Scalability: an org is scalable if it stays stable and performs well under rising demand without needing a redesign after a steep increase in workload.
Workload is anything that adds demand on org resources: simultaneous users, increased data, or complex transactions.
Supermarket analogy: scalability measures the 'cashiers' (capacity). When shoppers arrive faster than cashiers can serve them, queues grow and customers leave.
Large data volume (LDV): an excessively high number of records on a single object. It slows queries, search, list views and reports, and causes more timeouts.

LDV mitigations: data modeling and governance, an archival strategy, custom indexes, skinny tables, Salesforce Connect data virtualization, and avoiding data skew. Disable triggers during large loads where possible.
User registration rate: many on-demand sign-ups cause timeouts. Create user accounts in advance where possible.
Complexity of transactions: concurrent triggers, workflows, async batch jobs and sync jobs can cause record locking. Combine low-code and pro-code, and run non-critical batch and sync jobs off-peak.
Complexity of org: many custom components, roles, sharing rules and packages. Cyclical or recursive triggers can cause locking, so avoid them.
Role hierarchy: keep it under 10 levels of branches, don't mirror the org chart, and consolidate job titles into single roles by data-access level.
Sharing rules: limit ownership-based rules to 100 per object and criteria-based rules to 50 per object. Consider deferring sharing rule calculation during data loads.

Triggers: use one trigger per object with a naming convention that includes the object name. Bulkify triggers and helper classes to process up to 200 records per call, and use collections for DML and SOQL WHERE clauses.

Data skew: more than 10,000 child records under one parent. It slows queries, searches, list views, reports, dashboards and sandbox refreshes. Keep children per parent under 10,000 and spread new children across parents.
Ownership skew: one owner owns more than 10,000 records of a single object. It causes lengthy sharing recalculations when roles or groups change. Distribute ownership across more users.

Data governance: rules and policies ensuring data is usable, high quality and compliant. It covers creating, accessing and updating data, storage across clouds and on-premises, access for apps and monitoring tools, privacy ('right to be forgotten'), and archiving and destruction per retention schedules.
Data stewardship: the tactical roles that enforce the governance plan. A data steward owns data quality; a data custodian is the IT partner who knows how data is stored, structured and accessed.

A data management strategy should answer: what data, where stored, how much and growth rate, data movement, duplicate handling, ownership, access and security model, masking or encryption, and delete or archive policy.
Import step 1, prepare data: decide what belongs in Salesforce, map fields, export CSVs, load parents before children, and clean and de-duplicate first.
Data is a good CRM fit if Salesforce will be its system of record, key processes, automation, reports or KPIs depend on it, or users need activities, tasks, Chatter or Slack around it.

Import step 2, evaluate loading options: Data Import Wizard (up to 50,000 records, import only, in-browser); Data Loader (50,000 to 5 million records, import and export, external app); dataloader.io (cloud-based, powered by MuleSoft, varies by plan).
For LDV, Salesforce recommends Data Loader or an ETL tool configured to use the Bulk API, and deferring non-critical processes to speed loading.
Import step 3, sandbox testing: test in a full copy sandbox (a replica of production data and metadata) to uncover locking issues, duplicates and data errors.

Import step 4, load: choose the destination object, set matching criteria to prevent duplicates, specify the source file, map fields, review the error logs (CSV results) and check live data afterward.
Import step 5, schedule ongoing loads: pick real-time, batch or periodic loads (nightly, monthly, quarterly, annual), automate with Data Loader batch mode or an ETL tool, and plan for data growth.

Scalability testing measures how an app performs as demand grows and finds the point where it can no longer scale. Its attributes are response time, throughput, CPU usage, memory usage and network usage.

Load testing measures response time and customer experience under increased user demand. Its attributes are peak performance, server throughput, response time at various load levels below the breaking point, hardware robustness, and the number of users served without degradation.

Scale Center tracks org performance by examining user activity events and helps keep data secure. Key events to monitor: logins, logouts, search, URI, Lightning, Visualforce page loads, API calls, Apex executions and report exports.
Salesforce Data Mask protects sensitive data in sandboxes during testing.
principles: Build scalability into the design phase; retrofitting it later costs more and erodes user trust.
Scalability is about how data is structured and accessed, not only how much data exists.
Good scalability means better user experience, lower costs and greater agility, and it determines the lifespan of your org.
Keep parent-child ratios and record ownership balanced (under 10,000) to avoid data and ownership skew.
Keep automation simple and bulk-safe: one trigger per object, no recursive triggers, bulkified logic, and heavy jobs off-peak.
Govern data with clear policies, and assign a data steward and data custodian to enforce them.
Always load parent records before children, clean data first, and test in a full copy sandbox before loading production.
Match the loading tool to the data volume: Import Wizard for small loads, Data Loader or Bulk API ETL for large ones.
Performance testing is ongoing, not one-time. Use scalability and load testing plus Scale Center monitoring to keep refining the data strategy.

points: Large data volumes (LDV) can cause slower queries, slower search and list views, and slower sandbox refreshes; plan for them up front in the data model.
Data skew occurs when more than 10,000 child records are associated with the same parent record (or owner) in an org.
Account data skew: too many child records under one parent (e.g., an 'Unassigned' account) causes record locking and sharing performance problems.
Record locking: updating many contacts under one account in parallel locks both the contact and its parent account, so concurrent updates can fail.
Sharing issues: changing an account's owner may require re-examining every child record's sharing, including role hierarchy and sharing rules recalculation.

Ownership skew: a large number of records of one object owned by a single user; ownership changes are among the costliest transactional changes because sharing must be removed from the old owner, role-hierarchy parents, and sharing-rule recipients.
If ownership skew is unavoidable, make sure the skewed owner has no role so they and their records sit outside the role hierarchy and its sharing rules.

Lookup skew: a very large number of records point to a single record in the lookup object; Salesforce must lock the target record on every insert/update, causing lock exceptions with custom code plus LDV.
No tool specifically identifies lookup skew; look at objects with many records and heavy concurrent insert/update activity.
External objects map to data stored outside Salesforce, so data is accessed on demand rather than stored and synced, saving storage and avoiding LDV performance problems.
External data sources define how to reach external systems: Salesforce Connect for data, Files Connect for third-party content systems.

External objects support three relationship types: standard lookup (18-character record ID), external lookup (parent is external, matches on External ID standard field), and indirect lookup (child is external, parent is standard/custom, matches on a custom unique External ID field).

Salesforce search uses its own indexed data store; indexed search finds matches in the index, filters by permissions/limits, truncates the result set at a set size, then queries the database for displayed fields.
Selective list views, reports, and SOQL queries plus an understanding of query optimization are key to handling LDV.
SOQL queries child-to-parent (many-to-one) and parent-to-child (one-to-many) relationships; SOSL tokenizes multiple terms in a field and searches an index.

SOSL limits: up to 20 SOSL searches per transaction, and each search returns at most 2,000 records (250 for a single-object query without WHERE or ORDER BY). SOQL in the same transaction can return up to 50,000 records.

The Salesforce query optimizer exists because multitenancy prevents the database optimizer from optimizing alone; it keeps index statistics and runs pre-queries to decide whether an index helps, covering reports, list views, and SOQL.

Batch Apex is the best way to query and process large data sets asynchronously, up to 50 million records, but doesn't suit synchronous uses such as a Visualforce page needing more than 50,000 records.
A bulk query can retrieve up to 15 GB of data in fifteen 1 GB files and supports query and queryAll (queryAll also returns merged/deleted records and archived Task and Event records).

Bulk query processing: a query that doesn't finish within the two-minute timeout fails with QUERY_TIMEOUT; results over 1 GB or taking over 5 minutes to retrieve are cached and retried, failing after 30 attempts ('Retried more than thirty times'); results are stored for seven days.
A skinny table is a custom table holding a subset of fields from a standard or custom object, giving narrower rows, more rows fetched per database read, and exclusion of soft-deleted rows.

Skinny tables are synchronized automatically, used by the platform at query runtime without code changes, best for tables with millions of records, and available for custom objects and Account, Contact, Opportunity, Lead, and Case.
Skinny table caveats: adding a field or changing a field type requires Salesforce Customer Support to re-create the table; they are copied to Full sandboxes only.
Loading lean means including only the data and configuration needed for business-critical operations, and loading it as quickly as possible to reduce synchronization scope.
Lean loading steps: identify business-critical operations, identify the minimal data and configuration needed, define a strategy, and load quickly.

Defer-able setup that slows loads: private org-wide sharing defaults (use Public Read/Write and defer sharing calculation until after cutover), complex object relationships/lookups, sharing rules, and workflow rules, validation rules, and triggers.
Don't be too lean: keep parent records for master-detail children, record owners, and the role hierarchy in place during loading.
SOAP API suits real-time client apps updating a few records at a time and becomes unwieldy for large loads; Bulk API is REST-based and built to load or delete thousands to millions of records.
Bulk API benefits: fast processing, easy job monitoring, automatic retry of failed records, parallel processing, minimal API calls and round trips, and easy batch-size tuning.
Bulk API streams records into a job, stores them temporarily, slices them into user-defined batches (max 10,000 records), and processes batches in parallel or serially, each independently.
Suspending events involves three phases: analyze and prepare data, disable events for loading, and post-process.
Analyze/prepare: decide which requirements can be met by cleansing data before loading or sequencing loads, and which by post-processing (e.g., lookups, roll-up summaries).
Disable events: set validation, lead/case assignment, and territory assignment rules to inactive; for triggers, use a Custom Setting with a checkbox field that the trigger code checks before firing.
Post-processing: add lookups and roll-ups with Batch Apex or Bulk API, add foreign keys for integrations, reset trigger custom settings, and re-enable validation, workflow, and assignment rules.
Bulk API is useful for deleting and extracting LDV; its hard delete option suits processes deleting one million or more records.
Soft deletion flags records as deleted and moves them to the Recycle Bin; they still affect performance because queries must exclude them.
Recycle Bin data is kept 15 days or until the bin reaches a size limit, then physically deleted, or when the bin is emptied via UI, API, or Apex.
Bulk API hard delete bypasses the Recycle Bin so records are immediately eligible for physical deletion, freeing space sooner; it is disabled by default and must be enabled by an administrator.
Bulk API extract queries are split into 100,000-record chunks by default; the chunkSize header can set smaller or larger chunks up to 250,000.
At hundreds of millions of records, filtering by field values may return more rows than the optimizer's selectivity threshold, causing full table scans, slowness, or failure.
PK chunking splits bulk queries on large tables into chunks based on record IDs (primary key), which are always indexed.
Enable PK chunking for tables over 10 million records or when a bulk query consistently times out, using the header Sforce-Enable-PKChunking (e.g., chunkSize=50000).

PK chunking is supported for Account, Campaign, CampaignMember, Case, Contact, Lead, LoginHistory, Opportunity, Task, User, and all custom objects; each chunk is a separate batch counting toward the daily batch limit and downloaded separately.
With PK chunking, the original batch shows NOT_PROCESSED on success or FAILED on failure; a WHERE clause can filter, possibly returning fewer records than chunkSize.

Truncating a custom object quickly and permanently removes all its records while keeping the object and metadata; it also erases Recycle Bin records, history, and related events, tasks, notes, and attachments.
Enable truncation via Setup > User Interface > Enable Custom Object Truncate; a copy appears in Deleted Objects for 15 days, still counting toward limits.

You can't truncate standard objects, or custom objects referenced via lookup, on the master side of master-detail, used in reporting snapshots, having a custom index or external ID, or having active skinny tables.
principles: Design for scale from the start: keep child records per parent below 10,000 by creating enough parents and distributing new children across them.
Avoid dumping records on a generic owner or parent; skew turns routine operations into expensive locking and sharing recalculations.
When skew can't be avoided, minimize its cost (e.g., give the skewed owner no role).
Use data tiering and external objects when you have lots of data you rarely need at once, so it stays out of your org's storage.
Design selective queries, list views, and reports so the query optimizer can use indexes.
Process large volumes asynchronously (Batch Apex or Bulk API) rather than synchronously.
If indexes and best practices aren't enough, use skinny tables via Salesforce Customer Support, accepting their rigidity.
When a bulk query times out or fails repeatedly, simplify the query or use PK chunking.
Load only what is business-critical first, and defer everything else to after cutover.
Use Bulk API instead of SOAP API for large loads.
Temporarily suspending validations, workflows, and triggers is safe only if data is cleansed beforehand and enrichment is done afterward.
Keep essential structure (parents, owners, role hierarchy) intact while loading.
Remove data you no longer need, because soft-deleted records still hurt performance.
Use Bulk API hard delete for large deletions and PK chunking for very large extracts.
Use truncation to quickly purge test data from custom objects (it is irreversible).
Use these strategies regularly to keep LDV from degrading org performance.
